analysis.one_liner: Requires fenceline air pollution monitoring at 100 high-risk industrial facilities and posts the data publicly.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on December 17, 2025 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has received no hearing, no markup, and no vote; 23 House Democrats cosponsored it and no Republicans did.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the EPA to put emissions monitors at the fencelines of at least 100 industrial facilities that emit hazardous air pollutants like ethylene oxide, chloroprene, benzene, and formaldehyde — the chemicals linked to elevated cancer risk in nearby neighborhoods. It would force companies to publicly report what they emit, nearly in real time, and to take corrective action when pollution at the property line exceeds health-based levels. It would also expand the national air monitoring network, put at least 1,000 low-cost air sensors in overburdened communities, and restore the EJSCREEN environmental mapping tool. Federal cost is authorized at roughly $277 million over fiscal years 2026-27; the facilities themselves would bear the cost of monitors, reporting, and remediation.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near industrial polluters — often lower-income communities and communities of color near refineries, chemical plants, and plastics facilities. They would get publicly available, multilingual, near-real-time data on the toxic chemicals crossing their property lines, community alert sign-ups, and legally enforceable corrective action when fenceline levels are exceeded. Children and other vulnerable residents get explicit priority in monitor siting and health-based standards.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents near refineries and chemical plants

how_it_helps.text: Requires fenceline monitoring at a list of at least 100 high-priority polluting facilities, including at least 45 drawn from EPA Inspector General lists of facilities with high cancer risk, with monitoring data published online within 7 days of collection in a multilingual database [S2].

Requires industrial source categories to install continuous, real-time monitoring, sets fenceline corrective action levels for the top health-driving pollutants, and requires root-cause analysis, full remediation, and a public violation report when levels are exceeded [S2].

Requires public alert sign-ups so residents are notified when monitored emissions exceed peer-reviewed health reference levels, and requires the information to be publicized through local media in the affected communities [S2].

Expands the national monitoring network with 80 new NCore stations and 100 new regulatory-grade monitors, at least 40 of the stations sited in census tracts with elevated asthma, cancer, poverty, or multiple nearby polluters, plus 1,000 low-cost community air sensors [S2].
Bars the Administrator from granting any exemption from the bill's monitoring and corrective action requirements, and makes the requirements enforceable Clean Air Act obligations [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Facilities that emit hazardous air pollutants — chemical, petrochemical, refinery, plastics, metals, and waste-handling plants — would pay to install and maintain monitoring equipment, report emissions electronically, and remediate fenceline exceedances. Taxpayers fund the federal share: the bill authorizes about $277 million for EPA monitoring programs over fiscal years 2026 and 2027 [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes about $146 million, $50 million, $75 million, and $6 million in federal appropriations across its monitoring programs, which would fall on taxpayers unless offset [S2].

Monitoring and disclosure do not by themselves cap emissions; a facility can comply by measuring its pollution accurately while residents still breathe it, with health protection depending on how aggressively corrective action levels are set and enforced [S2].

The compliance burden — continuous monitors, 95-percent data uptime, repairs within 2 days, and remediation on exceedance — is significant for the covered facilities and their customers, and some costs could be passed to consumers in the prices of fuels and chemicals [S2].

The bill sets tight deadlines (monitors running within 18 months, a source list within 270 days) that depend on EPA staffing, and requires the agency to report how it will do the work without delaying other duties [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to exposed communities are concrete: publicly accessible data on toxic chemicals at their fencelines, alerts when levels exceed health benchmarks, and legally enforceable remediation when they do. The public cost is modest (about $277 million authorized). The main honest caveat is that this is a measurement and disclosure bill, not an emissions cap — it reduces pollution only indirectly, by making exceedances visible and legally actionable. On balance it is strongly weighted toward the residents who live downwind, with real but proportionate costs for industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in mid-December 2025, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on December 17, 2025 by Rep. Troy A. Carter of Louisiana with 17 original cosponsors [S1].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which is the only committee action in its history [S4].
23 House Democrats had cosponsored the bill as of the latest cosponsor record; no Republicans are listed [S3].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote has been scheduled or held, and the Congress remains in session [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one new: the industrial facilities the bill would monitor continue to operate under existing rules because the bill has not advanced past committee. If it stays there, facilities that emit hazardous air pollutants keep the current regime of limited fenceline data.

for.name: Rep. Troy A. Carter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which targets fenceline monitoring at industrial facilities including sources in his home state's petrochemical corridor.

for.name: 23 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republicans did.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on December 17, 2025 and has taken no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — as of the latest action record.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 cosponsors are House Democrats and the sponsor is a Democrat; no Republican support appears in the record, in a chamber where Republicans hold 223 of 440 voting-aligned seats.

industries.note: The bill names their source categories and NAICS codes directly for continuous fenceline monitoring, corrective action levels, and public reporting; companies like those emitting chloroprene and ethylene oxide in Gulf Coast communities would bear the heaviest compliance and remediation costs, which is the data that exposed residents want.

industries.industry: Petroleum refiners and marine loading operations
industries.note: Explicitly covered source categories; they would have to install and maintain continuous monitoring equipment and report emissions nearly in real time, with penalties for reporting lapses.

industries.industry: Plastics, rubber, primary metals, and waste management facilities
industries.note: Facilities in NAICS codes 322, 324, 325, 326, 331, 332, 339, 424, and 562 with accidental-release histories are squarely targeted for monitoring and corrective action requirements.

industries.industry: Air monitoring equipment and sensor makers
industries.note: The bill requires hundreds of regulatory-grade monitors and at least 1,000 low-cost community sensors, creating demand for monitoring hardware and services, a benefit that runs alongside the public's interest in better data.

analysis.trajectory: With the bill referred to a Republican-controlled Energy and Commerce Committee, no Republican cosponsors, and no committee action since its mid-December introduction, the likely path is that it never receives a hearing or a vote before the 119th Congress ends in January 2027 — the fate of most bills introduced without bipartisan sponsorship or committee support. It would need to be reintroduced to be considered in the next Congress.
